title: Floating-point subtraction
intro: Catch up on the key A Level ideas. Complete four retrieval questions, work through the examples, then practise and explain your reasoning.

questions.prompt: Why must floating-point exponents match before the mantissas are added directly?
questions.answer: Because corresponding mantissa bit positions must represent the same scaled place values .
options: Because corresponding mantissa bit positions must represent the different scaled place values .
Because corresponding mantissa bit positions need not represent the same scaled place values .
Because corresponding mantissa bit positions must represent the same scaled place values .
questions.feedback: Model answer: Because corresponding mantissa bit positions must represent the same scaled place values . Explanation: Aligning the exponents puts both operands on the same scale before the mantissas are added.

questions.prompt: Convert 01100000 1110 to denary. Use an eight-bit two’s-complement mantissa and a four-bit two’s-complement exponent.
Use 8-bit two’s complement to calculate 18 − 29 . Show how subtraction becomes addition.

blocks.title: Key vocabulary
items: Negation — Changing the sign of a value; in two’s complement, invert and add 1.
Cancellation — When subtracting similar values produces a much smaller result.
Guard bits — Extra low-order working bits retained during calculation.
Arithmetic right shift — A right shift that repeats the sign bit.
Renormalisation — Restoring a normalised mantissa while adjusting the exponent to preserve value.
Underflow — When a nonzero normalised result needs an exponent below the format’s minimum.

blocks.title: Align before subtracting
blocks.text: Choose a common exponent and use arithmetic right shifts to align the mantissas. Keep any low-order guard bits needed for an exact working result.

blocks.title: Negate the second mantissa
blocks.text: At the chosen working width, invert every bit of B’s aligned mantissa and add 1.

blocks.title: Add the aligned values
blocks.text: Sign-extend both operands to the same working width, add them, and interpret the signed result using the common exponent.

blocks.title: Handle cancellation, zero and range
blocks.text: A small difference may need left shifts and a reduced exponent to become normalised. Equal operands produce zero.
